rationale: Single-target novice learn session, taught then checked in a tight self-explanation cycle. One active idea is covered with one teaching block, one required free-response check, one repair, and one reexplain check, staying within time and avoiding deferred scope.

essentialIdeas: One glucose is split into two pyruvate and the net gain is two ATP and two NADH.
completionEvidence: State the net products of glycolysis from one glucose in your own words.
Correct a gap about the net outcome after the model.
Restate the outcome clearly after repair.

evidenceMap.essentialIdea: One glucose is split into two pyruvate and the net gain is two ATP and two NADH.

deferredContent: What net ATP from glycolysis is used for

methodBriefing.name: Feynman Technique
methodBriefing.what: Study a concise model, explain it in plain language, repair any gap, then explain it again.
methodBriefing.why: Explaining the relationship helps turn a memorized list into a usable mental model.
how: Answer from memory in your own words.
Compare your answer with the model and fix the missing part.
Give a second plain-language explanation without copying.
methodBriefing.completion: You can state the net products accurately, repair a missing part, and restate the idea clearly.
personalization: Keep each attempt short and concrete.
The first check is a free response because the session must produce the idea from memory.

activities.label: model
activities.title: Glycolysis outcome
activities.body: Read the model and note the net products. Then move on.

essentialIdeas: One glucose is split into two pyruvate and the net gain is two ATP and two NADH.

activities.label: explain
activities.title: Say the outcome from memory
activities.body: In your own words, name the net products from one glucose. Keep it to one short response.
activities.correctAnswer: One glucose is split into two pyruvate, with a net gain of two ATP and two NADH.
activities.feedback: A complete answer names two pyruvate, net two ATP, and two NADH. If one part is missing, repair the whole outcome together.

activities.label: repair
activities.title: Fix the missing part
activities.body: Use the model to correct any gap in your answer. Then give one corrected version.
activities.misconceptionSummary: Leaving out one of the net products or giving the gross ATP count instead of the net outcome.
activities.correctAnswer: One glucose becomes two pyruvate, and the net outcome is two ATP and two NADH.
activities.feedback: The correction should include all three net products and keep the net result, not the gross ATP made during the pathway.

activities.label: reexplain
activities.title: Restate the whole outcome
activities.body: Give a fresh explanation in plain language. Do not copy the model wording.
activities.correctAnswer: Glycolysis turns one glucose into two pyruvate and leaves a net gain of two ATP and two NADH.
activities.feedback: A strong restatement is complete, concise, and uses your own words. It should keep the split into two pyruvate and the net energy products together.

targetAssignments.essentialIdea: One glucose is split into two pyruvate and the net gain is two ATP and two NADH.

items.essentialIdea: Glycolysis converts one glucose into two pyruvate, producing a net two ATP and two NADH.

check.title: Glycolysis product balance
check.prompt: What is the net product outcome of glycolysis from one glucose molecule?
check.referenceAnswer: One glucose is converted into two pyruvate, with a net gain of two ATP and two NADH.
check.feedback: This combines carbon splitting with the net energy and electron carriers produced.

recognitionCheck.title: Glycolysis net result
recognitionCheck.prompt: Which statement best describes the overall outcome of glycolysis?
choices: One glucose becomes two pyruvate with a net gain of two ATP and two NADH.
One glucose becomes one pyruvate with a net gain of four ATP and two NADH.
Two glucose become four pyruvate with a net gain of two ATP and one NADH.
One glucose becomes two pyruvate with no net ATP gain and two NADH.
recognitionCheck.correctAnswer: One glucose becomes two pyruvate with a net gain of two ATP and two NADH.
recognitionCheck.feedback: The correct outcome includes two pyruvate plus the net ATP and NADH yield.
